cards.title: 2.1 Graphs of Square Root Functions
body: 2.1 Graphs of Square Root Functions

**Definition:** A **Square Root Function** is a real-valued function containing a radical with a variable in the radicand, primarily expressed in the form $$f(x) = a\sqrt{bx - h} + k$$, where the radicand $$bx - h \geq 0$$ and $$a, b \neq 0$$.

### Deep Dive
The parent square root function, represented as $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$, serves as the baseline for this entire class of functions. Unlike linear functions that extend infinitely in both directions or quadratic functions that form symmetric U-shaped parabolas, the basic square root graph resembles a curved ray that starts at a specific coordinate (the origin) and arches outward. This curvature is not arbitrary; it represents the inverse rate of growth compared to a quadratic function. cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: Horizontal stretch, compression, and reflection are controlled by the parameter $$b$$. If the coefficient inside the radical is positive ($$b > 0$$), the function curves to the right, toward positive infinity. However, if $$b < 0$$, the graph is reflected horizontally across the y-axis, causing it to curve to the left, toward negative infinity. This horizontal reflection is useful for modeling systems where the independent variable counts backward from a specific threshold, such as distance to a target or countdown timelines.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The period of a simple pendulum is governed by the square root function $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$, where $$L$$ is the length of the pendulum. This means that to double the swing time, you must quadruple the length of the string!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To find the starting point of any square root function quickly, set the expression inside the radical to zero and solve for $$x$$. The resulting value is the starting x-coordinate, and the constant outside the radical is the starting y-coordinate.

If $$a > 0$$, solving this inequality yields $$x \geq -\frac{b}{a}$$, meaning the domain extends to positive infinity. Conversely, if the coefficient of $$x$$ is negative ($$a < 0$$), the inequality sign flips when we divide, resulting in a domain of $$x \leq -\frac{b}{a}$$, which extends to negative infinity.

In the general transformed form $$f(x) = a\sqrt{b(x - h)} + k$$, the parameters $$a, b, h$$, and $$k$$ act as precise coordinates and shape modifiers. The horizontal shift is controlled by $$h$$, while the vertical shift is controlled by $$k$$. The starting point (or vertex-like anchor) of the graph is located at the coordinates $$(h, k)$$. Understanding this starting point is the first and most critical step in sketching any square root curve, as it establishes the boundary from which the function originates.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: In physical science and engineering, square root graphs are used to visualize and analyze non-linear relationships. For instance, according to Torricelli's Law, the velocity of fluid exiting a tank through an opening is directly proportional to the square root of the height of the fluid column ($$v = \sqrt{2gh}$$). Plotting this relationship allows mechanical engineers to predict fluid flow rates and design efficient drainage systems for water tanks, reservoirs, and chemical processing facilities.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: When the radicand contains a higher-degree polynomial, finding the domain requires a more detailed inequality analysis. For example, for a function with a quadratic radicand, such as $$f(x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 9}$$, we must solve the quadratic inequality $$x^2 - 9 \geq 0$$. Factoring the expression gives $$(x - 3)(x + 3) \geq 0$$. Performing a sign chart analysis reveals that the product is non-negative on the intervals $$(-\infty, -3]$$ and $$[3, \infty)$$, making this union of intervals the natural domain of the function.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: The vertical stretch, compression, and reflection are determined by the coefficient $$a$$. If $$a > 0$$, the curve arches upward from its starting point. If $$a < 0$$, the graph is reflected vertically across the x-axis, arching downward. This vertical reflection is common in physical contexts that model depletion, decay, or gravity-induced descent. The magnitude of $$a$$ determines the rate of this vertical arching; values where $$|a| > 1$$ stretch the graph vertically, while values where $$0 < |a| < 1$$ compress it.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: When sketching these functions, you can plot them quickly and accurately without a detailed table of values by following a simple three-step method: identify the starting point $$(h, k)$$, determine the direction of the horizontal and vertical arching based on the signs of $$a$$ and $$b$$, and plot one or two easy-to-calculate test points. This approach ensures a mathematically accurate curve while reinforcing how algebraic parameters translate directly into geometric transformations.

cards.title: 2.2 Domain and Range of Square Root Functions
body: 2.2 Domain and Range of Square Root Functions

**Definition:** The **Domain** of a square root function is the set of all real numbers for which the radicand is greater than or equal to zero ($$\geq 0$$). The **Range** is the set of all possible output values, restricted by the starting point and the direction of vertical opening.

### Deep Dive
Because square root functions are real-valued, they are subject to strict domain restrictions. In the set of real numbers, taking the square root of a negative value is undefined, as no real number multiplied by itself yields a negative result. Consequently, the expression inside the radical, known as the **radicand**, must always be non-negative. This algebraic requirement means we must restrict the domain of any square root function to ensure its inputs produce valid, real-valued outputs.

cards.title: Square Root Functions
body: Determining the range of a square root function depends on the starting point's y-coordinate and the sign of the vertical stretch factor $$a$$. Since the principal square root symbol $$\sqrt{\cdot}$$ always represents a non-negative value, the term $$\sqrt{bx - h}$$ is always greater than or equal to zero. Therefore, if the leading coefficient is positive ($$a > 0$$), the outputs must be greater than or equal to the vertical shift, resulting in a range of $$[k, \infty)$$. If the leading coefficient is negative ($$a < 0$$), the outputs are restricted to values less than or equal to the vertical shift, giving a range of $$(-\infty, k]$$.
